abstract: Nonexchangeable observations and order-sensitive model fitting break the usual symmetry argument for full conformal coverage. We extend split and full conformal prediction and jackknife+ by separating calibration weighting from tagged model fitting. Prespecified calibration weights in [0,1] emphasize observations believed comparable to the test point, while fixed tags let fitting exploit order. For full conformal prediction, a data-independent swap exchanges the test observation with an index sampled using normalized calibration weights and unit test weight before fitting. The swap links miscoverage to high-residual indices whose weighted mass cannot exceed alpha, without requiring symmetric fitting. Coverage is therefore at least 1-alpha minus a weighted sum of total-variation distances between original and swapped residual distributions; jackknife+ instead starts from 1-2alpha. Exchangeability eliminates this penalty, preserving validity. Under nonexchangeability, a small penalty limits undercoverage; distinct residuals and a small normalized test weight also limit overcoverage. Nonexchangeable simulations and ordered electricity data support complementary roles: calibration weighting improves coverage but widens intervals, whereas weighted fitting can shorten them. That width advantage disappears in the exchangeable, randomly permuted electricity control. Election coverage improves but remains below 90%, underscoring that arbitrary drift is not covered by a nominal guarantee.
methods: Unequal calibration weights and order-sensitive fitting obstruct the usual exchangeable-residual argument. Theorem 2b prespecifies weights w_i in [0,1] and algorithm tags t_i, normalizes the weights with unit test weight, and draws K independently of the data using these probabilities. Swap observation K with the test point before fitting, retaining positional tags; at the true test label, the test residual occupies position K in the swapped residual vector. Residuals above the swapped vector's weighted (1-alpha)-quantile carry total normalized weight at most alpha. The rejection test is unchanged if its threshold places the test weight at infinity; because w_i <= 1, this threshold dominates the swapped-vector quantile. Miscoverage thus requires K to be a high-residual index. Independence permits averaging over K. Comparing each swapped residual law with the original adds its total-variation distance; the original-law weighted mass is at most alpha. Miscoverage is consequently bounded by alpha plus the weighted distances.
results: Table 2 distinguishes coverage recovery through calibration weighting from interval shortening through fitting, at a 90% target. On ordered electricity data, keeping least squares fixed while weighting calibration residuals raises temporal-average coverage from 85.2% to 89.0%, but increases mean width from 0.565 to 0.606. With calibration weighting retained, weighted least squares gives 89.3% coverage and width 0.527: narrower intervals accompany slightly higher observed coverage, although both weighted methods remain below target. The randomly permuted, exchangeable version of the same data changes that comparison. Unweighted least squares, residual-weighted least squares, and residual-weighted weighted least squares attain 89.9%, 90.8%, and 90.8% coverage, with widths 0.639, 0.652, and 0.663, respectively. Thus weighted fitting provides no width advantage in the control, and weighting increases variability. These averages support complementary calibration and fitting roles on ordered data, not coverage at every prediction time. Arbitrary drift can produce a large weighted total-variation penalty between original and swapped residual distributions; the empirical gains therefore do not establish universal 90% coverage.
notes: Abstract and Methods retain the operative link: the pre-fit swap relocates the test residual to a sampled index, enabling a weighted-tail bound (Section 3.2; Theorem 2b proof). Results use Table 2's fixed-fitting and fixed-calibration contrasts, then the exchangeable permutation control. The WLS experiment cites equation (14), not the randomized-swap procedure (20); confirm implementation before assigning its theorem guarantee to the reported experiment. Table 2 contains temporal averages without uncertainty estimates; width units and significance were not inferred. The residual total-variation penalty is unmeasured. Jackknife+'s 1-2alpha baseline and the distinct-residual/small-test-weight conditions for limiting overcoverage remain explicit in the abstract.
